=== static-site-release.yml ===
name: Release static site

# THE ORCHESTRATOR of the static-website release standard — the one entry point
# every static-site repo of ours carries, vendored from the pack into this repo's
# own .github/ (GitHub resolves a reusable workflow or composite action only from
# the repo's own .github/, never from a mount). It owns the TRIGGERS and nothing
# else: the logic lives in the local reusable workflows it calls, and every
# repo-specific value comes from this repo's `.github/site.config` (read inside
# those workflows), so this file is copy-verbatim in every site repo.
#
# Release on push: any push to main that touches the repo's declared publish set
# cuts a release — bump the date-anchored version, tag it, deploy the site. A
# push that touches nothing published is a clean no-op, so ordinary README and
# tooling commits do not churn the version or redeploy an unchanged site.
#
# The dispatch form re-runs the same pipeline by hand; `force: true` releases
# even when nothing published changed (a rebuild after a settings fix, a first
# deploy on a repo whose site predates the pipeline).
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      force:
        description: "Release even when no published file changed"
        type: boolean
        default: false

# One release at a time, and never cancel one mid-flight: a cancelled run can
# leave the version bumped with no release or deploy behind it.
concurrency:
  group: static-site-release
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  release:
    permissions:
      contents: write   # push the version bump, create the release
      pages: write      # deploy the site
      id-token: write   # the OIDC token deploy-pages exchanges
      issues: write     # the failure reporter
    uses: ./.github/workflows/static-site-publish.yml
    with:
      force: ${{ inputs.force || false }}
=== static-site-deploy-pages.yml (first 40 lines) ===
name: "Static site: Deploy to GitHub Pages (reusable)"

# Deploys the repo's EXPLICIT publish set to GitHub Pages. Vendored from the
# static-website pack into the repo's own .github/; workflow_call ONLY — it is
# invoked by "Static site: Publish" at the released commit, so what is live is
# always exactly what was tagged. A repo never dispatches it directly.
#
# The artifact is assembled by the assemble-site composite action from
# `publish_root` + `publish_paths` — an additive list, so the agent-tooling dirs
# (.claude/, .claudinite/), dev tooling, notes and anything else unlisted are
# absent by construction rather than by remembering to exclude them. That also
# sidesteps the dangling-symlink trap that breaks a whole-root Pages upload:
# upload-pages-artifact tars with --dereference, and .claude/skills/* are
# symlinks into the gitignored corpus, empty on a runner.
#
# One-time owner setup in the calling repo: Settings → Pages → Source =
# "GitHub Actions". Until that is set, deploy-pages fails; the caller's failure
# reporter opens the tracking issue.
#
# The calling job must grant `permissions: contents: read, pages: write,
# id-token: write`.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Commit to deploy (empty = the default checkout)"
        required: false
        type: string
        default: ""

# Least privilege for a Pages deploy: read the repo, write Pages, mint the OIDC
# token deploy-pages exchanges.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never run two Pages deploys at once; let an in-flight deploy finish.
concurrency:
  group: pages
=== static-site-publish.yml (first 40 lines) ===
name: "Static site: Publish (reusable)"

# The logic behind every static-site repo's release, vendored from the
# static-website pack into the repo's own .github/. workflow_call ONLY — the
# `static-site-release.yml` orchestrator owns the triggers and passes no repo
# values; everything repo-specific comes from `.github/site.config` via the
# read-site-config composite action.
#
# The pipeline, in order — and the order is the point: nothing is bumped,
# tagged or deployed until the tests that guard the site have passed.
#
#   check    is a release due? A push that touched the declared publish set,
#            or `force`, or a repo with no release yet. The baseline is the
#            LATEST RELEASE TAG, not a time window, so a day whose run failed
#            is caught by the next push instead of stranded.
#   verify   the repo's own gate (`test_command`), on the tree being released.
#   bump     the date-anchored version (bump-site-version), pushed to main.
#            Pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN, which fires no workflow — hence the
#            explicit deploy call below rather than a second push trigger.
#   release  GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at the bump commit, with
#            auto-generated notes.
#   deploy   the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish
#            set.
#
# The caller must grant `permissions: contents: write, pages: write,
# id-token: write, issues: write`.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      force:
        description: "Release even when no published file changed"
        required: false
        type: boolean
        default: false

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

=== docs/product-spec.md head ===
# Fringe Discover — Product & Experience Brief

> A functional brief for a designer. It describes **what the product does, who it
> serves, and what information and decisions matter** — not how today's screens
> look. Treat the current interface as one possible answer, not a constraint.
> You are free (encouraged) to reinvent the form entirely.

---

## 1. The problem we're solving

The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is overwhelming by design: roughly **3,800 shows**
across **300-plus venues**, packed into three weeks, running from morning to
past midnight. The official programme is a catalogue — brilliant if you already
know what you want and are planning days ahead. It is useless to the person
standing on a street corner with a free hour, asking the only question that
actually matters in the moment:

> **"What can I go and see *right now*, near *here*, that I'd actually enjoy —
> and still make it to wherever I have to be next?"**

Fringe Discover exists for that person. It is not a planning tool for next week;
it is a **spontaneity tool for the next hour or two.** The festival's magic is
often accidental — stumbling into a show you'd never have booked. We want to
make that accident reliable.

### Who they are
- Visitors mid-festival, on foot, often without a fixed plan.
- People with a *gap*: between a booked show and dinner, or a free afternoon.
- Locals and tourists alike who are intimidated by the size of the programme.
- Decisive in the moment, not researchers — they want **a short list of good,
  reachable options**, not 3,800 search results.

The emotional target is **"delight + relief"**: the relief of the overwhelm
lifting, and the delight of a serendipitous find that still fits their day.

---

## 2. The core idea: reachability, not search

Most listings apps answer *"what exists?"* This one answers *"what can I make?"*

Three real-world constraints collapse the giant catalogue down to a handful of
genuinely actionable options:

1. **Where I am** (my location, right now).
2. **How far I'm willing to go and how** (on foot, bike, bus, taxi — and how
   many minutes).
3. **When I next have to be somewhere else** (a later show, a dinner, a train).

A show only earns a place in front of the user if it satisfies all three: it's
within reach, it hasn't already started (or only *just* has), and seeing it
still leaves enough time to get to the next commitment. Everything else is
noise and should disappear.

This is the heart of the product. **The single most important thing the design
must communicate is "can I actually make this?"** — and ideally how much breathing
room (slack) the user has if they go.
